content.title: Highlights from Artemis II’s Historic Journey Around the Moon
content.text: A record-breaking flight.VideoArtemis II Completes Historic Journey Around the MoonNASA’s Artemis II crew received a call from President Trump, who congratulated them for the successful lunar flyby.CreditCredit...Cassandra Klos for The New York TimesOn the sixth day, 248,655 miles from Earth, four people ventured farther from home than any human being who has ever lived.Embraced by the moon’s gravitational pull, four astronauts accelerated Monday afternoon on a path to swing around the lunar far side, five days after launching on the Artemis II mission from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida.“Today, for all humanity, you’re pushing beyond that frontier,” said Jenni Gibbons, a Canadian Space Agency astronaut who was the main point of contact for the crew at mission control in Houston.In response, Jeremy Hansen, a fellow Canadian who is a member of the Artemis II crew, hailed the space pioneers who had preceded them.“We most importantly choose this moment to challenge this generation and the next to make sure this record is not long-lived,” he said.A few hours later, Mr. Hansen, along with Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover and Christina Koch of NASA, became the first humans in more than half a century to slip behind the moon.ImageA view of Earth from the Orion capsule after it reached its farthest distance from the planet on Monday.Credit...NASA, via ReutersAt 6:44 p.m. Eastern time, video transmission from Artemis II blinked out, and the astronauts were cut off from the world’s other eight billion people. As the spaceship they named Integrity passed over the far side of the moon, they reached their greatest distance from Earth — more than a quarter-million miles — and their closest proximity to the moon at a bit over 4,000 miles.After 40 minutes of silence, the astronauts reconnected with humanity. From their windows, they watched as a thin crescent of sunlit Earth reappeared.“It is so great to hear from Earth again,” Ms. Koch said. Below them, facing the moon were Asia, Africa, Australia and the western Pacific.Ms. Koch described the beginning of a new era in which people would not only return to the moon but also build an enduring presence there.“But ultimately, we will always choose Earth,” she said. “We will always choose each other.”The astronauts’ Monday began with an unexpected voice — that of Jim Lovell, the pilot of Apollo 8, which orbited the moon in 1968, and the commander of Apollo 13, which set the previous record for the farthest distance traveled from Earth while making an emergency return.“Welcome to my old neighborhood!” Mr. Lovell said in a message recorded before he died in August.“It’s a historic day, and I know how busy you’ll be,” Mr. Lovell said. “But don’t forget to enjoy the view.”The astronauts did that.They also paused after passing the Apollo 13 distance record for the most emotional moment of the day. Mr. Hansen voiced the astronauts’ request to name two craters on the moon.One would be Integrity, after their spacecraft.The other would be to honor Mr. Wiseman’s wife, Carroll, who died in 2020 from cancer. “It’s a bright spot on the moon, and we would like to call it Carroll,” Mr. Hansen said, his voice cracking.ImageAstronauts embracing on Monday after naming a lunar crater “Carroll” in honor of the late wife of Reid Wiseman, the Artemis II commander.Credit...NASA, via Agence France-Presse — Getty ImagesThe astronauts embraced, and mission control observed a moment of silence as Mr. Wiseman’s two daughters looked on from the visitor gallery.The astronauts then prepared for the main event of their trip: hours of detailed observations of the lunar surface.A new photograph of the moon captured from Integrity shows a full view of the Orientale Basin, a dark, ringed 600-mile-wide crater that straddles the near and far sides of the moon. Human eyes had never before seen all of this feature.“Orientale just looks so dynamic right now,” Mr. Wiseman, the commander of Artemis II, said. “It’s very three dimensional.”Ms. Koch observed small craters formed recently by meteorites slamming into the moon. These impacts kicked up the lighter-colored soil beneath the lunar surface.“What it really looks like is like a lampshade with tiny pinprick holes and the light shining through,” she said. “They are so bright compared to the rest of the moon.”There was one more cosmic treat for the astronauts: a solar eclipse as the moon passed in front of the sun. The astronauts found it difficult to describe the sight when the moon was illuminated just from Earthshine — light reflected from our planet.“You can actually see a majority of the moon,” Mr. Glover said. “It is the strangest-looking thing that you can see so much on the surface.”ImageA new angle of the moon captured from Integrity shows a full view of the Orientale Basin, the dark, ringed 600-mile-wide crater that can be only partly seen from Earth.Credit...NASA, via Associated PressThe astronauts also counted five flashes of small meteors slamming into the lunar surface, delighting lunar scientists in mission control in Houston.In the dark background behind the sun, the astronauts also saw a reddish Mars and a Saturn with hints of orange.When the sun emerged from behind the moon, the long day of science ended.Then President Trump called. Among Mr. Trump’s questions: what was like when the astronauts were out of contact with the world.Mr. Glover said they were busy continuing their observations, but added, “I must say, it was actually quite nice.”President Trump said he would invite them to the Oval Office and ask for their autographs, noting that he rarely asks anyone for that.On the seventh day, the astronauts will mostly rest.ImageIn the Science Evaluation Room at Johnson Space Center during the Artemis II lunar flyby.Credit...Cassandra Klos for The New York TimesOn Thursday afternoon, Integrity will leave the moon’s embrace, and Earth will again exert a stronger gravitational pull on the spacecraft.The Artemis II astronauts will also chat with their colleagues on the International Space Station and recap their flyby observations with the science team at the Johnson Space Center.In the evening, the spacecraft may make a slight course correction burn to make sure they are on target for splashing down back on Earth on Friday.“I can’t believe it’s taken us so long to get back,” Jared Isaacman, the NASA administrator, said Monday night in Houston. “But here we are, and we’re never giving it up again. It’s just the start of a great journey.”President Trump calls the Artemis II astronauts after their historic journey.ImageArtemis II astronauts speaking with President Trump from their Orion spacecraft on Monday.Credit...NASAPresident Trump spoke with the astronauts of the Artemis II mission hours after their spaceship swung around the far side of the moon and took them farther from Earth than any humans on Monday.“You’ve made history and made all America really proud," Mr. Trump said, and later acknowledged the contribution of the Canadian member of the mission, Jeremy Hansen.The call celebrated a step toward ambitious goals Mr. Trump had set early in his first term of returning American astronauts to the moon and establishing a long-term base there. He declared in 2017 that “this time, we will not only plant our flag and leave our footprints,” but “establish a foundation for an eventual mission to Mars.”It will be years before another crewed Artemis mission is scheduled to land NASA astronauts on the moon. Indeed, Mr. Trump acknowledged that future missions, including the new moon landings, may be delayed past the end of his second term.But Mr. Trump projected confidence that “we’re going to be doing a lot of traveling” in space, and “you’re going to ultimately do the whole big trip to Mars.”The roughly 12-minute call offered a chance for levity and unity for Mr. Trump, who had only briefly acknowledged the mission since its launch on April 1. In public appearances and dozens of social media posts in the days since, Mr. Trump has focused his attention on the war with Iran.But in speaking to the astronauts, Mr. Trump made no mention of the war or his acrimony toward Canada. (“We like our neighbor,” the president remarked at one point.) The flags of the United States and Canada were prominently featured next to each other inside the Orion spaceship as Mr. Trump and Mr. Hansen, the Canadian member of the mission, exchanged compliments.“I spoke to a very special person, Wayne Gretzky, who I think you know, the great one,” Mr. Trump said to Mr. Hansen. “I spoke to your prime minister and many other friends I have in Canada. They are so proud of you.”And Mr. Trump, who is rarely in the position where he’s asking someone else questions, sounded genuinely curious as he asked the astronauts about their adventure. He appeared particularly interested in what it was like for the astronauts to be cut off from Earth in the brief window in which their ship slipped behind the moon.Victor Glover, the pilot on the mission, said, “I must say, it was actually quite nice.”At one point near the end of the call, Mr. Trump did not speak for just over a minute, giving the astronauts the impression that the connection may have been lost. The astronauts fussed with their microphone, which was constantly spinning in the capsule, as they waited. Then they asked if the president was still on the line.“I am, yes,” Mr. Trump said, his voice noticeably echoing. “I think we might have gotten cut off.” NASA controllers could be heard laughing in the background.Kenneth Chang contributed reporting from Johnson Space Center in Houston.AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTJared Isaacman wrapped up the Q&A by thanking the astronauts for taking us to the moon with them. “We are just honored to be a part of that,” Reid Wiseman said.When asked how this mission change’s humanity’s future among the stars, Victor Glover, the mission’s pilot said he had huge expectations for what’s coming next.Isaacman next asked what thoughts filled the astronauts’ minds when they were out of contact. The mission specialist Jeremy Hansen said they were so busy that they just tried to do a good job collecting science observations. But Reid Wiseman added they had a a brief moment eating maple cookies to celebrate Canada’s participation in Artemis II.Isaacman then asked what were some words that come to mind when the astronauts try to wrap their minds around this very unique experience.Christina Koch said: “Humility,” talking about all the people who came before.AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTNext question: what advice would you pass on to the Artemis III mission, which is to orbit the Earth and test docking with lunar landers in 2027. The pilot, Victor Glover, says they’ve been taking notes to pass on. How the astronauts pack is apparently very important. He also brought up the troubles with the toilet. Isaacman in response acknowledged, “We definitely have to fix some of the plumbing.”“What inspires you?” is the next question to the crew. Wiseman, noting he is now over 50, says it all comes back to family.Reid Wiseman, the mission commander said, “We’ve got to explore. We’ve got to go farther.”“I’m not ready to go home,” Christina Koch said, who noted how much fun she’s having in spite of the cramped quarters.AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTThe Artemis II astronauts are now doing another public event, answering questions posed by Jared Isaacman, the NASA Administrator, who is at Johnson Space Center in Houston.The phone call with Mr. Trump is over. Jared Isaacman, the NASA Administrator said, “That was pretty cool.”“I look forward to seeing you in the Oval Office,” President Trump said. He said he would ask for their autographs and that he doesn’t often ask for that.VideoCreditCredit...NASA, via The Associated PressAfter a long silence, the astronauts ask mission control if the president is still on the line.“I am, yes,” Mr. Trump said, eliciting laughter from the control room.AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTThe president is rarely in the position where he’s asking someone else questions. He sounds genuinely curious.“Did you see a difference, a big difference, between the far side of the moon and the near side of the Moon?” Mr. Trump asked the astronauts. “Was there a difference in feel? Or difference in look? What did you see?”VideoCreditCredit...NASA, via The Associated PressMr. Trump asked what it was like when the astronauts were out of communication with the rest of humanity. Victor Glover said, “I must say, it was actually quite nice.”President Trump asked the astronauts what was the most exciting thing about their journey today. Reid Wiseman, the Artemis II commander, responded by describing all of the things they saw today, such as the Orientale crater on the moon and the eclipse the crew witnessed after they went around the moon’s far side.President Trump congratulated the astronauts and said NASA would stay at the moon this time and then push on to Mars.AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTIn the background of the capsule, the flags of the United States and Canada are affixed to the wall next to each other. Below is the flag for the U.S.’s 250th birthday.All of the smiling astronauts just gave two thumbs up ahead of their event speaking to Earth.ImageCredit...NASAFor the past few minutes, the Artemis II astronauts been tidying up the Orion capsule they’re flying in, presumly for the event with President Trump. They also asked for fans to be turned down to reduce noise.In an abrupt announcement on social media just before 10 p.m., President Trump said he would be speaking “LIVE” with the Artemis II astronauts at 10 p.m.AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTThe hundreds of mementos aboard Artemis II include a flag that never made it to the moon.ImageThe Apollo Monument in Titusville, Fla., in January. The American flag that was selected to travel with the Apollo 18 mission, canceled by NASA in 1971, will travel with Artemis II on Wednesday.Credit...Cassandra Klos for The New York TimesWhen NASA canceled the Apollo 18 mission over 50 years ago, a flag it would have carried to the moon had already been selected. With the launch of Artemis II on Wednesday, it finally went to space.The flag is among hundreds of mementos and souvenirs that will be carried into space aboard the Orion spacecraft during Artemis II.The government canceled Apollo 18 because of budget cuts. Bringing its flag aboard Artemis II represents what Jared Isaacman, the NASA Administrator, wrote in a social media post is America’s “renewed commitment to return to the moon. This time to stay.”The Apollo 18 flag will be one of more than 200 American flags to fly on Artemis II, but it will be the only full-size flag at 3-by-5 feet.NASA has carried mementos on spacecraft since it first launched astronauts to space in the 1960s. Neil Armstrong went to the moon in 1969 with a piece of wood from the left propeller of the Wright brothers’ original Flyer.The Orion capsule, where the four astronauts are spending their 10-day lunar flyby, will continue the tradition by carrying 10 pounds of mementos and other trinkets that honor America’s history of air travel and space exploration.Other notable mementos include a one-square-inch swath of muslin fabric from the Wright Flyer and a copy of an image from the first spacecraft to successfully transmit close-up images of the lunar surface back to Earth.Because Jeremy Hansen, a Canadian astronaut, is aboard the mission, the Canadian Space Agency also packed its own mementos. Those include stickers and patches promoting the agency and a Canadian flag.There will also be 100 silver Snoopy pins tucked into the flying kit. NASA astronauts present these pins to employees who demonstrate “exceptional contributions to flight safety and mission success,” according to the agency. Each pin depicts Snoopy, the beloved character from Charles M. Schulz’s comic strip “Peanuts,” in a spacesuit.Eclipse observing is complete.Science is signing off for the night. “You really brought the moon closer for us today, and we cannot say thank you enough,” Kelsey Young, who leads the Artemis II science team, said from mission control.AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTAdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTAdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTThe first earthlings to the moon weren’t humans. They were tortoises.ImageZond 5 after splashdown in the Indian Ocean; Soviet scientists examining the tortoises flown around the moon aboard Zond 5.Credit...RKK Energiya When people think of the first visitors to the moon from Earth, a couple of names might come to mind: Neil Armstrong, the first human to walk on the moon, or Bill Anders, who took the iconic “Earthrise” photograph.Far fewer people remember the tortoises.On Sept. 15, 1968, as the Soviet Union and the United States were in a fierce race to send the first astronauts to the moon, the Soviet Union successfully launched the Zond 5 spacecraft.The Soviet space program had already beat NASA in a number of biological firsts: It sent the dog Laika around the Earth in 1957 and then followed man’s best friend with a man, Yuri Gagarin, in 1961, and Valentina Tereshkova, the first woman to orbit the Earth, in 1963.Zond 5 extended to the moon the Soviet streak of firsts. It carried a payload of fruit flies, plants and two Russian tortoises, also known as steppe tortoises, that scientists would later use to study the effects of lunar orbit on living organisms. Steppe tortoises, native to the dry deserts and grasslands of Central Asia, were picked for the experiment because they were easy to secure on the spacecraft.Approximately two weeks before the launch date, the tortoises were placed in the capsule without any food, so scientists could study the effects of starvation in space. Each tortoise weighed about 12 to 14 ounces before the flight.After a seven-day journey, Zond 5 re-entered Earth’s atmosphere and splashed down in the Indian Ocean. Despite the rough sea landing, the tortoises survived.It took several days for the spacecraft to be recovered and returned to Moscow, where scientists discovered that the tortoises had lost about 10 percent of their body weight and experienced more tissue atrophy compared with a couple of starved tortoises that did not venture to space and served as a control group.Soviet scientists concluded that “the main structural alterations in the tortoises were caused by hunger and only to a lesser extent by space flight factors,” according to a Soviet study published in 1969.The Zond 5 mission occurred at a challenging moment for NASA. The agency was facing budget cuts and was under pressure to send men to the moon before the Soviets did. The agency’s administrator, James E. Webb, announced the day after Zond 5 launched that he was resigning in a pointed news conference.“What this really means is we are going to be in a second position for some time to come,” he said in regard to the space program’s financial restrictions.But while the tortoises were the first earthlings to fly by the moon, NASA was not far behind. Three months later, Apollo 8 became the first mission to take humans around the moon and back, bringing the United States one step closer to a moon landing.AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTAdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTAdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTThe crew will see a solar eclipse while on the far side of the moon.ImageThe crew of Artemis II will have a chance to see a solar eclipse, but it may not look like the Great American Eclipse of April 2024.Credit...Ashley L. Conti for The New York TimesThe astronauts will spend roughly seven hours gazing deeply at the moon during their lunar flyby on Monday. And for 53 minutes, they will take a break from lunar observations to instead study the sun.A total solar eclipse will be visible from the Orion spacecraft, which has been named Integrity. The moon will pass in front of the sun from the spacecraft’s point of view, blocking its light. That will give the astronauts a chance to observe part of the corona, the sun’s wispy outer atmosphere.Had the astronauts lifted off too far into the launch window, they would have missed the eclipse. But lifting off on April 1 gave them the unusual opportunity to observe the cosmic event for an extended period of time.On Earth, solar eclipses occur when the moon moves between our world and the sun. Because the moon and sun appear to be the same size in the sky, this shields the solar surface from view, revealing the sun’s corona.It’s a little different on Integrity. From the crew’s vantage point, the moon will appear much larger than the sun, so the astronauts will only be able to see a portion of the solar corona.“That is very, very unique to this mission,” Kelsey Young, an Artemis II science officer, said in a news conference on Saturday.She added that the lunar flyby includes science objectives designed around observing the sun’s activity during the eclipse, which will help scientists better understand how the sun works and affects the entire solar system.Dr. Young wore eclipse earrings while speaking to reporters on Sunday about what else the astronauts would be able to spot during the event, including Mercury, Venus, Mars and Saturn. They may also see the glow of our planet faintly illuminating the near side of the moon, an effect known as Earthshine.The eclipse will end when the sun pops back out from behind the moon — a lunar sunrise just for the crew.AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENT
